fact: Since the 1970s, over 200 frog species have been considered to be extinct.
As of 2015, there are over 6000 different frog species that have been discovered.
Frogs have 3 distinctive cavities in their bodies that host their organs.
The liver of a frog contains 3 lobes which help secrete its digestive juices called bile.
Frogs can hold their breath for an average of 4 to 7 hours at a time.
Frogs lay their eggs in the water much as toads do.
The Goliath Frog is said to be the largest species of frogs in the world.
Frogs and toads are not considered to be the same animal but are considered to be similar.
The smallest frog species in the world is known as the Paedophryne amanuensis .
The largest organ in the body of a frog is its liver.
Many frogs have special toe pads that allow them to stick onto surfaces without falling.
In some eastern countries, frogs are typically consumed as street food or in prepared dishes.
The skin of a frog can vary in color from green, brown, black, orange, blue, and many others.
Frogs are classified as social animals that typically live in groups referred to as an army.
Frogs have two slits at the bottom of their mouths that allow them to croak with their vocal cords.
There are approximately 170 different types of poison dart frogs.
The tongue of a frog is typically ⅓ of the length of its body.
Around 466 frog species are classified to be critically endangered.

One of the most common animals seen in the world are frogs. Despite their size, frogs are considered to be quite the opponent in the wild due to their excellent survival and camouflage skills. Frogs are also an important part of the food chain as they are both the predator and prey. Find out more about these cute and slimy creatures with our collection of frog facts.

The Darwin’s frog is a small frog species that are typically classified by their elongated snout which gives their head a triangular appearance. When a female Darwin’s frog lays its eggs , the male will guard them for a period of 3 to 4 weeks by storing them in its vocal cords until the embryos begin to move.

The tadpoles inside the male frog will feed off of their egg yolks and other secretions that are produced by the wall of the vocal sac until the stage of metamorphosis. Once this stage has been reached, the tadpoles will have turned into frogs by then and jump out of their father’s mouth and disperse.

The Bornean flat-headed frog is classified as an endangered frog species that originate from the rainforests of Indonesia . This frog species is also believed to have evolved from the plethodontid salamanders that originate in Mexico and have been discovered to have no lungs inside of their bodies.

According to research, red-eyed tree frogs typically mate through October until March of the next year and are usually done by a male attracting a female of its species by croaking. When the eggs of this species hatch, the fluid found inside the eggs allow the tadpoles to be washed into the water below them.

Once the eggs have hatched, the tadpoles take about an average of 14 weeks until they develop limbs and organs and become small frogs. The red-eyed tree frog is more commonly known for its bright green skin and vivid red eyes with vertical pupils similar to that of a snake .

Frogs are best known for their outstanding jumping ability granted by their long and powerful legs which are often used to escape predators in the wild. The frog species that holds the world record for the highest jump belongs to the South African sharp-nosed frog which has an average body length of 3 inches and can jump over 130 inches in a single leap or jump.

However, despite the jumping abilities of these creatures, not all species of frogs can jump as high as other species due to some of them having shorter legs than others. If a person was to jump this high, the average 5-foot tall person would need to jump over 220 feet in a single leap.

According to research, several species of frogs create nests out of foam for their eggs which keeps them safe from diseases and prevents the development of fungus. These nests are often made under leaves and over a body of water so that when it is time for the eggs to hatch, the tadpoles can fall into the water immediately.

During the first few weeks after hatching, the mother frog typically feeds each of its tadpoles with different types of algae from plants and surfaces. Additionally, tadpoles are also able to eat other decaying animals, plants, and on rare occasions, other frog eggs as well for the necessary nutrition they need to grow.

The golden poison dart frog is considered to be one of the most deadliest and poisonous animals on the planet. The poison of this frog species comes from their skin which makes them deadly to touch with your bare hands as the skin can absorb the poison on the frog’s body.

The poison from this frog often causes nausea, swelling to the infected area, and as well as a paralyzing effect on the body’s muscles. The poison that comes from the golden poison dart frog is said to be strong enough to kill a grown man within 10 minutes from the initial exposure to the body’s bloodstream .

The Guajira Giant Glass frog is well-known for being one of the few glass frogs that share transparent skin types. According to research, the reason why these creatures have transparent skin is still unknown.

However, it is believed that this unique skin type may be due to evolutionary survival which helps these creatures hide from predators in the wild by blending into their surroundings much like a chameleon does when it changes its skin color. Glass frogs can typically be found in Southern Mexico and as well as in the Central and South America regions where there are around 60 different types of glass frog species.

Female and male frogs typically have different sized markings on their ears which is known as the tympanum which often helps us in determining their gender more simply. In the majority of frog species, male frogs typically have larger ears while females have smaller sized ones.

Additionally, the gender of a frog can also be determined by their body size , nuptial pads on their hands, and as well as if they sing or not. Other factors such as skin color and how loose their skin is can also help others determine if a frog is a boy or a girl.

One of the easiest ways to determine if these amphibians are classified as a toad or a frog is by looking at their legs. Frogs are typically smaller and have longer legs used for jumping which allows them to escape from prey and move around locations quicker.

On the other hand with toads, their legs are typically shorter and they hop around from one place to the other instead of jumping taller heights. Additionally, frogs and toads can also be differentiated by their skin when frogs tend to have more moist-looking skin while toads typically have dry and hard looking skin types.

Typically, frogs will have teeth located on the upper part of their jaw which help them while hunting and consuming their prey. One species of frog is noted to have teeth in either jaw however and it is known as the Gasthrotheca Guentheri frog which is native to South America.

Despite typically swallowing their prey whole, some frogs will use their teeth to help chew down their food to swallow better. The teeth found on the upper jaw of a frog are referred to as the Maxillary teeth and some frogs will also have small teeth on the roof of their mouths called the vomerine teeth.

According to research, a few poisonous frog species obtain their poison traits from the foods they eat such as insects that contain toxins and chemicals within their bodies. However, these frogs can eat these insects without suffering from any type of damage towards themselves.

One of these poisonous frogs includes the blue poison dart frog whose diet mainly consists of ants and other small insects that carry toxins in their bodies from the plants that they consume before falling prey to these frogs. Lastly, depending on the species of the frog, the toxicity level of its poison may vary as well.

According to statistics, the average frog typically lives for about 10 to 12 years whereas frogs that are kept in captivity may live as long as 15 years old. During this time frame, a frog will go through four different stages throughout its life where first it is an egg, followed by the tadpole stage, to a froglet, and finally as an adult frog.
Some more recent research has also shown that the Goliath frog can also live up to 15 years in the wild due to its large size while in captivity they may live as long as 21 years old.

Frogs are scientifically classified as carnivorous animals which indicates that apart from insects, they may also consume other animals including other frogs. In some cases, frogs may also physically fight each other by biting and jumping onto each other.

Additionally, certain frog species may also eat their eggs and tadpoles, and as well as other frog’s offspring if they cannot find any other source of food. According to scientists, the African clawed frog favors the taste of its tadpoles compared to other prey such as insects.

The Lilliputian frog is a newly discovered species of frog that originates from the Zongo Valley in Bolivia . This frog species is considered to be fairly small measuring 10 mm long and is considered to be talented in camouflaging itself from enemies.
According to scientists, this species of frogs is considered to be one of the smallest in the world and as well as the smallest amphibian.
Not all species of frogs have teeth on their upper jaw that help them chew their food. As a result, these slimy critters usually swallow their prey whole when they hunt or when they are given food.

Frogs are equipped with long sticky tongues that allow them to quickly capture their prey and curl them down to the back of their throats to swallow whole. On average, frogs typically eat twice a day and their diets will usually consist of insects, fruits, plants, and other small creatures. Full-grown frogs can go long periods without eating whereas froglets typically need to eat daily to survive.

According to scientists, the bones of a frog from a new ring each year during hibernation much similar to the way that trees grow a new ring as it ages. Additionally, these rings on their bones can, later on, be counted to determine the age of the frog in question.

During the winter, frogs typically go towards the bottom of bodies of water that are rich in oxygen where they will lie on top of the mud for the whole duration of the winter. By doing so, the frog allows the oxygen from the surrounding area to be absorbed by its skin as the rest of its body systems slow down to survive the hibernation process.

Frogs have several different types of calls and sounds that they use to communicate and gain the attention of other frogs. Typically, only the males make use of these calls for courting rituals and announcing their location to defend their territory.

The sounds that a frog makes can travel clearly through the air, water, and as well as through substrate which shows how audible their calls can be. The male frog can create their croaking sounds thanks to the two slits that form in the bottom of their mouth which opens the vocal pouch that allows air to pass through and create noise.

Over the years, frogs have become a popular choice for exotic pets as they can be kept in simple living conditions that often come inexpensive. Pet frogs are typically fed a variety of live insects which are fairly easy to collect or buy from your local pet store.
Common species of pet frogs are Ranids and Leptodactylidae . Additionally, other species that are considered to be rarer are typically sold for a higher price than common frogs.

Before someone is allowed to legally purchase a glass frog as a pet, they must first meet several requirements and understand the tedious care instructions for these slimy creatures. Glass frogs typically require large amounts of vegetation in their tanks for them to feel comfortable and avoid overstressing them.

For owners that wish to own a pair of glass frogs, a larger tank is required as they each need to feel uncrowded inside the tank. Depending on the species of the glass frog, the required size of the tank can vary as this species requires a large amount of space to be kept properly.

Herpetology comes from the Greek word herpeton which translates into ‘reptile’ or it can also mean ‘creeping reptile’. This study is concerned with reptiles in general including not only frogs, but newts, salamanders, reptiles, and caecilians as well.

A person who studies herpetology is referred to as a herpetologist and these people typically have a background in life sciences such as biology or zoology. On average, it takes about 4 years to complete a bachelor’s degree in this field before entering a master’s program in herpetology.

Frogs and toads share many things in common such as their appearance, abilities, and other aspects including their carnivorous diets. These two species are also members of the same scientific class, Amphibia, which classify both of them as cold-blooded amphibians.

Both species also spend their early life in the water and begin from eggs and into tadpoles until they develop organs and limbs to be able to live on land. However, despite their similarities, frogs, and toads secrete different types of chemicals from their skin that can cause discomfort towards the other party and cause fights among each other or harm to their health.

A new study that was conducted in 2020 stated that both frogs and salamanders can glow in the dark under specific lighting conditions. In this study, over 32 different species of amphibians were tested to which all came out positive to be able to re-emit the light that comes from either blue or ultra-violet lighting.

This process is referred to as biofluorescence which is a phenomenon observed to be present in several other life forms as well such as jellyfishes and turtles . Scientists have also observed that not only does the skin of frogs and salamanders glow after absorbing special light, but their bones and urine does as well.

According to scientists, the wood frog that is native to Alaska typically freezes around two-thirds of their body water into ice and causes their blood to stop flowing and their hearts to stop beating as well. However, during this occurrence their glucose levels are found to rise significantly which allows them to tolerate temperatures as low as 0 degrees celsius.

It is stated that the snow helps these frogs provide an insulated layer for themselves that allows them to stay frozen for long periods to survive hibernation and the consistently cold weather in Alaska. Once spring arrives, the frogs begin to thaw and turn as much glucose as they can from their bodies back into glycogen and urinate the excess amounts of it to be ready for mating season.

The Surinam toad is known to have a special method of mating compared to other frog species. Typically, the male frog will call the attention of the female by creating clicking sounds underwater until a female approaches it and releases around 60 to 100 eggs.

As the eggs are released, the male frog will fertilize them and push the eggs onto the back of the female which will allow them to stick firmly on. Once the eggs on the female’s back hatch, these frogs will begin a life of solitude again until it is time to mate once more. On average, it takes around 105 days for metamorphosis.

Frogs and toads often swim in a similar manner where it can be compared to the breaststroke that humans use at times to swim. Frogs will draw their hind legs up towards their bodies and propel themselves forward by kicking out their legs and repeating the process to continuously swim around in a straight line.

Because these creatures are amphibious, frogs still need air to breathe which means that they might drown if they allow their lungs to be filled up by water. However, frogs typically breathe by absorbing the oxygen found in the water, if there is no oxygen to be found where they are swimming they will not be able to breathe.

When frogs begin to mate, it takes the female around an average of 4 days to lay its eggs before it can leave the water. After mating with a female, the male frog immediately looks for another female to mate with and will continue this pattern until the mating season passes.

Frogs typically begin mating as soon as they come out from hibernation which explains why the sign of spring typically indicates loud singing coming from frogs in forest areas and ponds. They come out when rain and melting snow begin to create puddles which will help keep their bodies in a temperature above freezing point.

Scientists have discovered that frogs rely on their hearing solely for distinguishing other frogs and as well as their predators. Apart from this function, it seems that the brain of the frog does not react to anything other than acoustic patterns that are needed to distinguish as a means to survive.
Some studies determine that this may be due to the lack of physical ears that frogs have despite having ear holes that are located right behind their eyes.

Despite how strange it may sound, frogs routinely do this as a means of not wasting precious protein found in the shredded skin ratchet than just leaving it behind to rot or taken by other animals. When a frog sheds, it pushes all the skin towards its mouth to make the process faster and easier to consume at the same time.

According to research, older frogs will shed their skin around four times each year while younger frogs will tend to shed their skin more often every few weeks or so and some as often as daily for some species.

Also scientifically known as the Phyllomedusa sauvagii , this frog species is unique from others as it is the only frog that can create wax. This frog species is native to South America and can also be found in other places such as Bolivia, Brazil , and as well as Paraguay where it breeds during the rainy seasons of the year.

The wax that these frogs produce is also considered to be poisonous to other creatures which means that they can be deadly to the touch as this wax is spread around its body to moisturize itself. Thanks to this trait, this acts as a strong defense mechanism against predators and other creatures.

Frogs have a special feature in their bodies called a ‘drinking patch’ which they use to absorb water through their skin. This gland is located right at the underside of the frog’s stomach and thighs.

For people taking care of frogs, water given to these little critters must be dechlorinated and placed into a bowl that they can easily come in and out from. Additionally, they must not be given tap water as this could kill them otherwise due to the possible chemicals that may come from the pipes or the water source of the tap water.
A frog is an amphibian. They lay their eggs in water. The eggs hatch into a tadpole which lives in water until it metamorphoses into an adult frog.
Tadpoles look more like fish than frogs, they have long finned tails and breathe through gills.
An amphibian can live both on land and in water.
Although frogs live on land their habitat must be near swamps, ponds or in a damp place. This is because they will die if their skin dries out.
Frogs breathe through their nostrils while also absorbing about half the air they need through their skin.

Frogs use their sticky, muscular tongue to catch and swallow food. Unlike humans, their tongue is not attached to the back of its mouth. Instead it is attached to the front, enabling the frog to stick its tongue out much further.
The common pond frog is ready to breed when it is only three years old.
Frogs in the wild face many dangers and are lucky to survive several years. In captivity however, frogs can live for much longer.
Frogs can see forwards, sideways and upwards all at the same time. They never close their eyes, even when they sleep.

Remarkably, frogs actually use their eyes to help them swallow food. When the frog blinks, its eyeballs are pushed downwards creating a bulge in the roof of its mouth. This bulge squeezes the food inside the frog's mouth down the back of its throat.

A frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura [ 1 ] (coming from the Ancient Greek ἀνούρα , literally 'without tail'). Frog species with rough skin texture due to wart -like parotoid glands tend to be called toads , but the distinction between frogs and toads is informal and purely cosmetic, and does not reflect taxonomy or evolutionary history.
Different species of frog use a number of methods of moving around including jumping , running , walking , swimming , burrowing , climbing and gliding .

frog , any of various tailless amphibians belonging to the order Anura . Used strictly, the term may be limited to any member of the family Ranidae (true frogs), but more broadly the name frog is often used to distinguish the smooth-skinned, leaping anurans from squat, warty, hopping ones, which are called toads .

The snout-vent length of frogs ranges from 9.8 mm (0.4 inch) in the Brazilian Psyllophryne didactyla to 30 cm (12 inches) in the West African Conraua goliath . The male anuran is generally smaller than the female.

Fossil anurans are known from the Jurassic in Europe, North America, and South America, extending through the Pleistocene. Given the extensive radiation of many anuran clades, the fossil record is somewhat poor, with several families lacking any fossil representatives. Several fossil genera have not been assigned to recognized families. The superorder Salientia includes the fossil "proto-frog" Triadobatrachus , from Madagascar, and Anura.
Frogs are ectothermic animals that rely on external heat sources to regulate their body temperature.
Frogs absorb water through a specialized permeable patch of skin on their belly rather than drinking through their mouths.
Most frogs have a transparent nictitating membrane that slides across the eye to protect it while swimming.
Frogs detect sound through a tympanic membrane, visible as a round disc located just behind each eye.
The skeleton of a frog contains no ribs, a defining feature of all members of the order Anura.
Frogs have four fingers on each front limb and five toes on each hind limb.
A frog's tongue is attached at the front of its jaw and flips outward rapidly to capture prey.
Frogs exchange gases through their moist skin as well as their lungs, a process called cutaneous respiration.
The skin of a frog must remain moist at all times for cutaneous respiration to function properly.
Frogs lack a diaphragm and inflate their lungs using a buccal pumping mechanism driven by the throat.
Some frog species possess small vomerine teeth on the roof of the mouth used to grip struggling prey.
Frogs have a three-chambered heart consisting of two atria and one ventricle.
The eyes of a frog are positioned high on the sides of its head, providing a very wide field of view.
Male frogs of most species are the only ones that vocalize, using calls to attract mates and defend territory.
Some frog species estivate during hot or dry seasons, burying themselves underground in a dormant state.
Frogs typically swallow their prey whole, using their front limbs to push larger items further into their mouths.
Frogs produce several types of vocalizations including advertisement calls, release calls, and distress calls.
The African clawed frog was historically used as a human pregnancy test, as females lay eggs in response to human pregnancy hormones.
The tomato frog of Madagascar inflates its body and secretes a sticky white mucus when threatened by predators.
The purple frog of India was unknown to science until 2003 and spends nearly its entire life underground.
The Chilean four-eyed frog displays two prominent false eye spots on its rump to startle potential predators.
The Titicaca water frog is fully aquatic and has large loose skin folds that increase surface area for absorbing dissolved oxygen.
The Amazon milk frog produces a white milky secretion when stressed, which gives it its common name.
The Vietnamese mossy frog has bumpy green skin that closely mimics the appearance of moss-covered rocks.
More than one third of the world's known amphibian species are currently classified as threatened with extinction.
Amphibians are experiencing population declines faster than any other class of vertebrates on Earth.
The introduction of the American bullfrog outside its native range has contributed to the decline of native frog species worldwide.
Most tadpoles are herbivorous, grazing on algae and aquatic plant matter before metamorphosing into carnivorous adults.
Some frog species undergo direct development, hatching from eggs as fully formed miniature frogs with no tadpole stage.
The male Darwin's frog broods developing tadpoles inside his vocal sac until they are ready to emerge as froglets.
Male frogs grip females during mating in a position called amplexus, which can last from minutes to several days.
Frog eggs lack a hard shell and must be deposited in water or very humid environments to survive.
A mass of frog eggs laid together is called spawn, which may contain from a few to tens of thousands of eggs.
Warmer water temperatures generally cause frog eggs to develop and hatch more quickly than cooler conditions.
The golden poison dart frog of Colombia secretes batrachotoxin, one of the most potent naturally occurring toxins known.
Poison dart frogs raised in captivity without their natural diet of alkaloid-rich insects do not develop their characteristic toxicity.
Indigenous Choco peoples of Colombia traditionally coated blowgun darts with secretions from poison dart frogs for hunting.
Many poison dart frogs sequester their chemical defenses from alkaloids found in the mites and ants they consume.
The adhesive toe pads of tree frogs work through wet adhesion and capillary forces rather than suction cups.
Some frog species store elastic energy in their tendons before launching a jump, enabling acceleration beyond what muscles alone produce.
Each frog species has a unique advertisement call that females use to identify and locate potential mates of the same species.
Frog calls are produced by forcing air from the lungs across vocal cords and into an amplifying vocal sac.
Some frog species produce ultrasonic calls above the range of human hearing to communicate in noisy environments.
Frogs play a dual ecological role as predators of invertebrates and as prey for birds, snakes, fish, and mammals.
The loss of frog populations is often followed by population increases in the mosquitoes and insects they previously controlled.
Tadpoles are important algae grazers in freshwater ecosystems that help regulate aquatic plant growth.
The African clawed frog Xenopus laevis was one of the most widely used laboratory animals of the 20th century.
Skin secretions from frogs have been investigated as potential sources of antimicrobial peptides active against drug-resistant bacteria.
The compound epibatidine, isolated from the skin of an Ecuadorian poison frog, prompted research into novel non-opioid painkillers.
The Wallace's flying frog has greatly enlarged webbed feet that allow it to glide significant distances between trees.
The African bullfrog is one of the few frog species in which males are consistently and substantially larger than females.
The Puerto Rican coqui has been introduced to Hawaii where its nighttime calls have become a significant invasive nuisance.
John Gurdon's 1962 frog cloning experiments laid the foundation for nuclear reprogramming research, earning him the 2012 Nobel Prize.
Some frog species have been recorded living at altitudes above 4,000 meters in the Andes and Himalayan mountain ranges.
Herpetologists can survey the frog species present in an area using acoustic monitoring alone, identifying each by call.
The African clawed frog can detect vibrations in water using a lateral line system similar to that found in fish.
The gastric brooding frog of Australia swallowed its fertilized eggs and suppressed its own digestion to brood young in its stomach.
The gastric brooding frog is now considered extinct, having disappeared from Australian waterways during the 1980s.
Scientists are attempting to resurrect the gastric brooding frog through de-extinction genetic techniques in a project called the Lazarus Project.
Tadpoles raised in the presence of predators tend to develop deeper tail fins, which improve their escape swimming performance.
The chemical secretions of frog skin have inspired the development of several pharmaceutical compounds in research settings.
The magainin peptides discovered in African clawed frog skin were among the first antimicrobial peptides identified in any vertebrate.
The Kihansi spray toad was declared extinct in the wild in 2009 after a dam altered the spray zone habitat it depended on.
The Kihansi spray toad has since been successfully bred in captivity at US zoos with the goal of eventual reintroduction.
Some frog species exhibit geographic variation in their calls, with populations in different regions producing distinct acoustic dialects.
Male frogs calling from elevated positions broadcast their calls farther than those calling at ground level.
The Pristimantis genus of South American frogs contains over 500 described species, making it one of the largest vertebrate genera on Earth.
New frog species continue to be formally described at a remarkable pace, with dozens of previously unknown species named each year.
The common frog of Europe typically returns to breed in the pond where it was born, guided by chemical cues in the water.
Frogs have been found preserved in amber from the Cretaceous period, providing information on ancient amphibian ecology.
The ancestor of modern frogs is thought to have first appeared approximately 250 million years ago, before the dinosaurs.
The clawed frogs of Africa in the family Pipidae have no tongue and use their clawed feet to push food into their mouths.
The African clawed frog acts as a healthy carrier of chytridiomycosis, spreading the fungal disease to native frogs where it is introduced.
Frogs in urban areas have been documented adjusting the timing and pitch of their calls to reduce interference from traffic noise.
Some frog species modify their call pitch in response to competing males, reducing acoustic overlap and improving signal clarity.
The leaf-litter frogs of the tropics are among the most camouflaged animals on Earth, being nearly invisible on the forest floor.
The hairy frog of Cameroon has hair-like skin filaments on its flanks that may increase surface area for cutaneous respiration.
The hairy frog can force broken toe bones through its toe pads to produce sharp defensive claws when threatened.
The Surinam toad embeds fertilized eggs into pockets in the female's back skin, where they develop until fully formed toadlets emerge.
The gray tree frog of North America can shift its skin color between gray and green to match different resting surfaces.
The gray tree frog survives winter freezing using glucose and glycerol as natural antifreeze compounds in its tissues.
The spring peeper is one of the first frogs to call in spring across eastern North America, often beginning while ice is still present.
Spring peepers survive winter by partially freezing, using glucose accumulation to protect their cells from ice damage.
The wood frog has the northernmost range of any North American frog, extending well into the boreal forests of Alaska.
The wood frog's heart stops beating while it is frozen solid in winter, resuming function as the frog thaws in spring.
In ancient Egypt, the frog goddess Heqet was associated with fertility, childbirth, and the creation of life.
Frog legs are a commonly consumed delicacy in France, China, Vietnam, and Indonesia.
The international trade in frogs for human consumption involves hundreds of millions of individual frogs harvested annually.
Some cultures traditionally place frogs in milk because frog skin secretions have mild antimicrobial properties that slow souring.
The red-eyed tree frog is one of the most widely recognized and photographed frog species in the world.
The thyroid hormone is the primary driver of metamorphosis in frogs, triggering tail resorption and the development of limbs.
Tadpoles can detect chemical signals released by predatory fish and modify their behavior to reduce predation risk.
The ornate horned frog of South America has powerful jaws capable of gripping and holding prey nearly its own size.
Frogs have two separate hearing organs: the basilar papilla for higher frequencies and the amphibian papilla for lower frequencies.
The green and black poison dart frog is one of the most commonly kept amphibians in captivity worldwide.
The moor frog of Europe displays striking sexual color change during the breeding season, with males turning vivid blue.
The burrowing frog uses a hardened tubercle on each hind foot to excavate burrows by digging backwards into soil.
Frogs in cold climates accumulate glucose and other cryoprotectants in their tissues before the onset of winter freezing.
Some frog species breed explosively, with thousands of individuals gathering at a single location over just a few nights.
The tailed frog of western North America is the only frog known to achieve internal fertilization using a tail-like appendage.
The tailed frog's tadpoles have specialized sucker mouths that allow them to cling to rocks in fast-flowing mountain streams.
The crab-eating frog of Southeast Asia is one of the very few amphibians capable of surviving in brackish coastal water.
Frogs typically shed their outer skin layer periodically and then consume it, recycling the nutrients it contains.
Some frog species lay their eggs inside rolled leaves above water so that hatching tadpoles fall directly into the pool below.
The giant African bullfrog actively defends its nest of eggs and tadpoles, charging large animals that come near.
Male bullfrogs in North America defend calling territories, with dominant males occupying the most productive egg-laying sites.
Frogs in the genus Ceratophrys, known as Pacman frogs, are capable of biting hard enough to break human skin.
The blue poison dart frog is endemic to a small area of Suriname and is among the most popular frogs kept in terrariums.
Some tadpole populations exhibit cannibalism when crowded into temporary pools with limited food resources.
The strawberry poison dart frog exhibits over 30 color morphs across its range in Central America.
The common toad produces bufotoxins from parotoid glands behind its eyes that are harmful and distasteful to most predators.
Foam nests created by tree frogs protect eggs from desiccation, temperature extremes, and bacterial and fungal infection.
The Indian bullfrog undergoes dramatic seasonal color change, with males turning bright yellow during the breeding season.
The Asian horned frog has leaf-shaped projections and a triangular profile that makes it nearly invisible on the forest floor.
Some frogs time their breeding precisely to the onset of monsoon rains, emerging from underground dormancy within hours of rainfall.
The male tungara frog adds complex acoustic elements called chucks to its call when competing males are nearby.
Some frog species coordinate their embryo hatching in response to vibrations that indicate a predator is approaching.
The Bornean flat-headed frog is the only known frog species that has no functional lungs, breathing entirely through its skin.
Rain frogs of southern Africa have very rounded bodies and walk rather than hop, unlike most other frog species.
The shovel-headed tree frog uses a bony head shield to plug the entrance to the hollow branch where it shelters.
Some frog eggs contain symbiotic algae within the egg capsule that photosynthesize and provide oxygen to the developing embryo.
The fire-bellied toad arches its back to display its brightly colored underside as a warning signal when threatened.
The paradox frog of South America holds an unusual record: its tadpoles can reach 25 cm while adults measure under 7 cm.
The breeding calls of some large frog species can be heard from distances of several kilometers on calm still nights.
Some species of tree frog spend their entire lives within the water trapped in a single bromeliad plant.
Male frogs that call at higher rates attract more females but also draw more attention from predatory bats and snakes.
Frogs are among the most speciose groups of terrestrial vertebrates, with over 7,000 described species as of recent counts.
Frogs in the family Microhylidae, the narrow-mouthed frogs, are among the most diverse frog families with hundreds of species.
The African clawed frog has been introduced to many countries through the aquarium trade and escaped laboratory specimens.
The red-eyed tree frog embryo can detect the vibrations of an approaching snake and hatch early to escape into water below.
The glass frog male often guards his clutch of eggs on the underside of a leaf, keeping them moist with his body.
Some large Ceratophrys horned frogs are capable of remaining motionless for days at a time while waiting for prey.
The mountain chicken frog of the Caribbean islands was named for the chicken-like flavor of its meat when cooked.
The mountain chicken is critically endangered due to chytridiomycosis and overhunting on the islands of Dominica and Montserrat.
Many frog species produce breeding calls that peak in intensity during and immediately after rainfall events.
The shovel-nosed frog of sub-Saharan Africa feeds primarily on termites and ants, excavating their mounds with its snout.
Frogs are featured in the myths and folklore of nearly every culture that inhabits regions where frogs are found.
The marsupial frog carries developing embryos in a dorsal brood pouch, from which fully formed froglets eventually emerge.
The harlequin frogs of the genus Atelopus suffered catastrophic population crashes across Central and South America from chytridiomycosis.
The flying frogs of Southeast Asia belong to multiple independent evolutionary lineages, demonstrating convergent evolution of gliding.
Frogs played a key role in the history of physiology when Galvani's 18th-century experiments on frog legs led to the discovery of bioelectricity.
The golden tree frog of Trinidad is endemic to a small area of cloud forest and depends on bromeliads for breeding.
Some male frogs produce satellite calls near the territory of a dominant male to intercept females attracted by his call.
The Darwin's frog has a triangular head and pointed snout that helps it blend into leaf litter on the forest floor.
Frogs of the family Ranidae, the true frogs, are found on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.
The southern gastric brooding frog went extinct in 1981, just over a decade after its stomach-brooding behavior was first described.
The word amphibian comes from the Greek amphibios, meaning living a double life, referring to their aquatic and terrestrial phases.
Frogs are more diverse in tropical regions, where warmth, moisture, and vegetation support far more species than temperate zones.
Some arid-zone frogs have evolved waterproof skin that drastically reduces water loss, allowing them to thrive in desert environments.
The waxy monkey tree frog of South America secretes a lipid layer across its skin to waterproof itself against dry air.
The waxy monkey tree frog actively basks in sunlight during the day, an unusual behavior enabled by its waxy waterproofing.
Some frog species form aggregations of tadpoles that swim together in schools, which may help reduce individual predation risk.
The African running frog trots on its limbs rather than hopping, an unusual locomotor strategy among anurans.
Some male frogs wrestle rival males during territorial disputes, with larger individuals winning access to prime calling sites.
Frogs that breed in temporary water bodies must lay eggs that develop quickly before the pool evaporates.
The common African foam nest tree frog creates large communal foam nests above water alongside multiple other females.
Frogs have been documented adjusting their buoyancy underwater by regulating the amount of air retained in their lungs.
Frogs often congregate in large groups called choruses, where the combined sound attracts females from a wider area.
The Australian green tree frog is one of the few frog species to successfully adapt to living around human dwellings.
The Australian green tree frog produces skin secretions that have been investigated for potential antibacterial pharmaceutical uses.
The Pipa pipa Surinam toad can embed up to 100 eggs into specialized pockets in the skin of the female's back.
When Surinam toad young are fully developed, they burst through the pockets in their mother's back as miniature fully formed toads.
Frogs are highly sensitive to climate change because their ectothermic physiology responds strongly to even small temperature shifts.
Rising temperatures are altering the timing of frog breeding seasons, causing mismatches with peak insect availability.
Some frogs can receive sound both through their tympanic membrane and through their lungs, which act as a secondary sound receiver.
The pumpkin toadlet of Brazil is one of the few known frogs to fluoresce visibly under ultraviolet light.
The pumpkin toadlet's fluorescence was discovered when researchers examined specimens under UV light during a biofluorescence study.
Frogs have an unusual visual system that responds strongly to moving targets but is relatively unresponsive to stationary objects.
The mossy frog of Vietnam plays dead when threatened, lying motionless with its limbs curled until danger passes.
Some frog species produce both airborne calls and substrate vibrations simultaneously when communicating with potential mates.
Frogs of the genus Nanorana on the Tibetan Plateau are among the highest-altitude anurans recorded in the world.
Frogs often congregate near artificial lights at night to ambush the insects that are attracted to the light source.
Fossil evidence shows that frogs survived the mass extinction event at the end of the Cretaceous period 66 million years ago.
Some populations of leopard frog in North America have been found with extra or missing limbs, linked to parasites and pollution.
The discovery of limb abnormalities in North American frogs in the 1990s raised public awareness of the impact of agricultural runoff.
The African reed frogs of the genus Hyperolius display vivid patterns of yellow, green, red, and black warning coloration.
Some horned frogs of South America consume earthworms, centipedes, and other frogs larger than their own head width.
Frogs have been used to test water quality in laboratory settings because their embryos are sensitive to environmental contaminants.
Some tree frogs of Australia cluster together in shaded tree hollows during summer days to avoid heat and desiccation.
The Corroboree frog of Australia is one of the very few frogs known to synthesize its own alkaloid toxins rather than obtaining them from prey.
The Corroboree frog is among the most strikingly patterned frogs in the world, with vivid yellow and black stripes.
Some frogs migrate significant distances at the onset of the dry season to reach permanent water bodies where they can survive.
Frog reintroduction programs have been launched on multiple continents to restore populations lost to disease and habitat destruction.
Citizen science platforms are increasingly being used to document frog populations and track range changes in real time.
The red-eyed tree frog uses its vivid red eyes in a startle display called deimatic behavior to surprise approaching predators.
Some male frogs produce calls that alternate with neighboring males to reduce acoustic masking and improve signal transmission.
The common water frog of Europe is actually a naturally occurring hybrid between the pool frog and the marsh frog.
Frogs in the genus Allobates in South America are non-toxic but mimic the coloration of toxic poison dart frogs to deter predators.
The desert rain frog of southern Africa produces a remarkably high-pitched squeak as a defensive call when threatened.
The African bullfrog can aestivate underground for up to several years during extended droughts, waiting for rainfall to return.
Some tree frogs absorb water from rain on leaf surfaces by pressing their bodies flat against leaves during rainfall.
The Panamanian golden frog produces a toxin called zetekitoxin that is among the most potent amphibian toxins ever identified.
Frogs in the family Bombinatoridae, the fire-bellied toads, flash their bright red or orange undersides as a warning display.
The turtle frog of Australia is a burrowing species that feeds almost exclusively on termites in underground colonies.
Some frogs in temporary pools can accelerate their development dramatically, compressing metamorphosis into a matter of days.
The glass frog's transparent belly skin allows observers to see the beating heart and developing eggs inside the living animal.
Some Amazonian frog species lay their eggs in the water trapped in fallen Brazil nut pods on the forest floor.
The spotted tree frog of eastern Australia has declined sharply and is now classified as endangered within its restricted range.
Many frog species show high site fidelity, returning to the same breeding location year after year throughout their adult lives.
The coqui frog of Puerto Rico produces a two-note call where the first note repels rival males and the second attracts females.
Frogs have been documented at cave entrances and in dim subterranean environments, though few species are fully cave-dwelling.
Some female frogs of dendrobatid species actively compete with other females for access to high-quality male territories.
The tomato frog's white mucus secretion causes allergic reactions in some predators, discouraging repeated attacks.
The giant waxy monkey tree frog of South America is the largest member of its genus and is popular in the exotic pet trade.
Chytridiomycosis disrupts the frog's ability to absorb electrolytes through its skin, ultimately causing cardiac arrest.
Some frog species undergo hormonal changes during drought that trigger burrowing behavior and the secretion of a protective cocoon.
The water-holding frog of Australia has been used by Aboriginal Australians as an emergency water source during desert travel.
Some tropical frogs are active during the day rather than at night, particularly those that are brightly colored and toxic.
The red-backed poison frog of Amazonia transports its tadpoles one at a time on its back to individual water-filled leaf axils.
Frogs of the family Hemisotidae burrow head-first into soil using a hardened snout, unlike most burrowing frogs that dig backwards.
Some frog species have been found to adjust the dominant frequency of their calls in response to ambient noise in urban environments.
